title: Befriend Everyone
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating compassion and respect in our interactions with others, particularly when we disagree or have differing perspectives. By recognizing our interconnectedness and accepting others as they are in the present moment, we can begin to bridge the divides that often lead to polarization and conflict. This requires a shift from judgmental and reactive communication to a more mindful and non-judgmental approach, allowing us to connect with others on a deeper level and create positive change.
topics: Buddhist teachings on interconnectedness and compassion
Abraham Lincoln's grief over Willie's death
universal nature of sorrow and suffering
Soto Zen principles of presence and non-judgmental awareness.

sentences.text: Good evening.
I brought my own flashlight in case it gets too dark.
The title of my talk is Befriend Everyone.
This past February, I read a very interesting article in the New York Times about how public discourse has degraded over the course of our unusual elections in the U.S., Britain, and even France.
I decided then to develop a talk on this subject.

Tonight, I want to read a couple of excerpts from this article and talk about how we might return to speaking respectfully to those with whom we differ, and how we might return to regarding everyone—strangers and familiars—as friends.
I've chosen this topic not because I've mastered how to do this, far from it, but because I think it is worth learning how to do, how to befriend everyone.
As we know, Buddhism teaches us that everyone has Buddha nature.
Buddha nature, the capacity to become wise and compassionate, is inherent in human beings.
Buddhism also teaches that everyone is interrelated.
Through our interactions, we co-create each other.
In effect, we make each other up as we interact.
I am as much the way you see me as I am the way I see myself, and the same for you.
My interpretation of you causes me to behave in a certain way toward you, and you behave back toward me in a certain way in response.
We make each other up as we go.
Even when we try very hard to drop our preconceptions of each other, as Buddhism teaches, we still affect and shape each other.
We are intertwined, inter-created.
It's sometimes appalling, but it's true.
Here's a pertinent quote about how this works more broadly.
It really boils down to this: *All life is interrelated.
We are all caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied together into a single garment of destiny.
Whatever affects one directly affects all indirectly.
We are made to live together because of the interrelated structure of reality.* Who do you think said that?
I had never heard it before and ran into it.
Our interactions are also reciprocal.
If I help you, I help myself.
If I harm you, I harm myself.
If you harm me, you harm yourself.

Because he who harms me harms himself, it makes sense for me as a Buddhist to be compassionate, not angry toward the person who harms me, and to wish him well and that he doesn't do this anymore for his own sake.
The Tibetan Buddhist teaching arising from their belief in reincarnation is that at some time or another, everyone has been our mother.
Because our mothers have given us life, we must be grateful and honor them.
Likewise, we must honor everyone who has at one time or another been our mother.
So how do we take these Buddhist teachings into our daily life?

Today in our society and in much of the world, we are experiencing angry factionalism, tribalism, political polarization, name-calling, blaming, abusive language, incivility in public discourse, and loss of compassion for those who are less fortunate.
Our fall election painfully pointed out that we Americans are each in our own informational bubble, making it difficult for us to understand, let alone accept, the perspectives of others.

It's my sense that the current public climate of abusive speech is in part an unintended outcome of our communications technology: TV, email, Facebook, smartphones, Twitter, chat face, or whatever that is.
I don't know what it is, but I know what's going on out there.
These all allow us to speak to each other without being in the presence of the person we're speaking to.
This technology enables us to speak without consequences we feel, experience that.
In fact, it even encourages us to do so.
Because we aren't physically present with the person we're texting or writing in some way, we don't have the advantage of seeing their reaction to us to let us know how it's coming across.
So it's easy to forget to consider the impact of our words or photos and what they might have on our readers or viewers.
In fact, gradually over time, we have forgotten what we say through the media does affect others.
Given our communications technology and also the highly emotional political turbulence in our society and the world today, it's hard to remember that everyone is a Buddha.

When we experience online, when we experience online and through our clever devices that our political or moral values and beliefs are being attacked, but we don't want to react, what are we to do instead?
Do we have to capitulate to the person we feel insults our beliefs or us?
To get along, do we have to give up our beliefs?
Do we have to stop thinking or caring about moral or ethical issues?
Sometimes these feel like the only options.
But the answer to these now common dilemmas is no, though not simply no.
As the Buddha taught about everything in our experience, the key is to accept our situation as it is.
That is, when we're polarized, when we're afraid, we don't know quite what to do to make things better.
Well, we can turn again to Buddhist teachings and also to conflict resolution models, which tell us to seek to understand and accept the other person's current reality, where they are coming from.
Put aside our own views for the moment until we better understand the other person's views, listen to what's underneath his words and emotions.
By accepting others as they are in the current moment, we allow them to open and to change, perhaps in the future.
Is this easy to do?
No.
Sometimes it feels impossible.
We're triggered by what feels like abusive language or attitudes.
Our immediate reaction is to push back.
Here are a couple of stories I want to read you this evening from an article by Rachel Cuss, the one I mentioned that I read in February.
A British novelist who has published this long article, and it's titled The Age of Rudeness with a subtitle as a social contract phrase.
What does it mean to be polite?

She's writing out of the context of that big argument that went on in Britain about whether they should stay in the common market or leave it, and there was a lot of heated language, if you might remember, from news reports.
In her novels, this writer whose name is Rachel Cuss is fascinated with language and meaning, and she writes very interestingly about people through their conversations and miscommunications.
She wrote this article to explore the cultural upheaval in Britain that led to that vote to get out of the European common market.
The first story Cuss tells is about being in a British airport online at passport control.
She observes with surprise and annoyance the passport control official shouting at each passenger as he directs them to the correct lines.
She writes, *In a world as unmannerly as this one, how is it best to speak?* She says, "There's no need to be rude," I say to the man in the packed hall at passport control.
"There are people everywhere, and his job is to send them to the right queues.
I have been watching him shout at them.
There's no need to be rude," I say.
His head jerks around.
"You're rude," he counters.
"You're the one who's rude."
This is an airport, a place of transit.
There are all sorts of people here, people of different ages, races, and nationalities, people in myriad sets of circumstances.
In this customs hall, there are so many different versions of living that it seems possible that no one version would ever be agreed upon.
Does it follow, then, that nothing that happens here really matters?
"No, I'm not," I say.
"You are," he says.
"You're being rude," unquote.
Nonplussed, Cuss moves on to eventually get onto her plane.
Another week later, sometime later, a second incident happens at another British airport.
Cuss this time is with a friend, waiting to show their carry-on luggage to a security official.
Here is what happens, she writes: *Another day, another airport.
This time the situation is clearer.
My country has recently voted to leave the European Union, and rudeness is rampant.
People treat one another with a contempt that they do not trouble to conceal.

The people in uniforms, the airport officials, exercise their faux power with uncommon ugliness, while the rest of us look suspiciously at one another, not sure what to expect in this new unscripted reality.
The uniformed woman at security bangs the gray plastic trays one after another onto the conveyor belt with a violence that seems to request attention.*
The person in front of me in the queue is a well-roomed black woman.
She is traveling with a child, a pretty girl, a pretty young girl with a neatly plaited hair.
She has put two large clear bags of cosmetics and creams in her tray.
The uniformed woman halts the queue and slowly and deliberately holds up the two bags, looking fixedly at their owner.
"What's this then?" she says.
"What's this about?"
The woman explains that because two of them are traveling, she has assumed that they are entitled to two bags.
Her voice is quiet and polite.
The little girl gazes ahead with wide, unblinking eyes.
"You assumed wrong," the uniformed woman says.
"You don't get away with that," she says, grimacing and shaking her head.
"Where do people like you get your ideas from?"
The rest of us watch while she makes the woman unpack bags and then decide which of her possessions are to be thrown away.
They are mostly new and expensive-looking cosmetics.
The woman's fingers are shaking as she scrabbles with the various pots and jars.
She keeps dropping things, her head bowed, her lower lip caught in her teeth.
The uniformed woman's unrepentant commentary on these events is so unpleasant that I realize she is half demented with what would seem to be a combination of power and powerlessness.
No one intervenes.
I do not inform her that there is no need to be rude.
My traveling companion, a painter, is the politest person I know, but I have noticed that he does not often take up arms on another person's behalf.
He dislikes conflict.
When it is our turn in the queue, the uniformed woman stares at the bag he has placed in the tray.
It contains his tubes of paint.
They are crumpled and be spattered with use, and there are so many of them that the bag can't close at the top.
She folds her arms.
"What are these?" she says.
"They're paints," he replies.
"You can't take those through," she says.
"Why not?" he asks pleasantly.
"The bag has to close at the top," she says.
"That's why not."
"But I need them to paint with," he says.
"You can't take them through," she says.
He looks at her in silence.
He is looking directly into her eyes.
He stands completely quiet and still.
The look goes on for a very long time.
Her eyes are small and pale blue and impotent.
I did not notice them until now.
My friend neither blinks nor looks away, and the woman is forced to hold herself there as the seconds tick by.
Her small eyes open and straining.
During these seconds, it seems as if the layers of her are being removed.
She is being simplified, put in order, being looked at.
He is giving her his full attention, and I watch the strange transformation occur.
Finally, he speaks.
"What do you suggest I do?" he says very calmly.
"Well, sir," she says.
"If you're traveling with this lady, she might have room in her bag."
Neither of them looks at me.
They are still looking at each other.
"Would that be acceptable?" he says.
"Yes," she says.
"I don't see why not."
I proffer my bag, and the woman herself transfers the paints from one bag to another.
Her hands labor to do it with care and exactitude.
It takes her a long time.
Finally, she seals the bag and lays it gently back in the tray.
"Is that all right, sir?" she says.

Now that he has won this victory, I want him to reprimand her, not just for her behavior toward the black woman in the queue, but for all the wrongs her behavior represents, for the fact that it's safer to be him, and always has been.
He does not reprimand her.
He smiles at her politely.
"Thank you very much," he says.
"It would have been a shame to throw them away, wouldn't it?" she says.
"Yes, it would," he says.
"I appreciate your help.
I hope you enjoy your holiday, sir," she says.
Amazing story.
As the story indicates, simply being with an angry or frustrated person, accepting them as they are in the moment, can diffuse a situation.
It takes time and patience to do this, and a task that's especially difficult in a crowded airport processing line.
It takes empathy.

As Sherry Turkle in her book, *Reclaiming Conversation*, she's a sociologist at MIT who studies technology, actually, and is talking about the effect of technology on our culture and particularly young people as to how we don't communicate face to face anymore.
She says, "The empathic relationship does not begin with the sentence, I know how you feel.
It begins with the realization that we don't know how another feels.
We should begin with the invitation, tell me how you feel."
In this story, Cuss's friend just gazes at the official, stays with her until the woman realizes that he actually is seeing her, is there with her.
He doesn't know her, so he doesn't try to malign her with words.
He just gazes kindly at her.
In effect, he befriends her.
In the way of the Bodhisattva, Shantideva, he has something to say about how we see and befriend those who are strangers or whom we don't know.
This is in the chapter on meditative concentration, a few quatrains here: *Strive at first to meditate upon the sameness of yourself and others.
In joy and sorrow, all are equal.
Thus be guardian of all as of yourself.
The hand and other limbs are many and distinct, but all are one, the body to be kept and guarded.
Likewise, different beings in their joys and sorrows are, like me, all one in wanting happiness.
This pain of mine does not afflict or cause discomfort to another's body, and yet this pain is hard for me to bear, because I cling and take it for my own.
And other beings' pain I do not feel, and yet because I take them for myself, their suffering is mine, and therefore hard to bear.
And therefore, I'll dispel the pain of others for it is simply pain, just like my own, and others I will aid and benefit, for they are living beings like my body.
Since I and other beings both in wanting happiness are equal and alike, what difference is there to distinguish us that I should strive to have my bliss alone?
And since I and other beings both in fleeing suffering are equal and alike, what difference is there to distinguish us that I should save myself and not the others?*
In our world today where there's a lot of frightening and puzzling things going on, I believe we need to learn ways to think of each other as friends, to befriend each other.
Perhaps it's the artist way we must adopt to look and look until we see without judgment or opinion, until the other person feels seen and begins to see us as well.
I have an artist friend, a man even older than I am.
He lives in Portland.
He's been an artist and art teacher for years and years, and he's still productive.
He's like eighty-six or seven, and he has a show every year in his gallery.

He's really remarkable, and I was visiting him and his wife some months ago, and because we were all getting less able to walk all over the city, we were driving around to see sights that we hadn't seen before or I hadn't seen before.
And he would be attracted to something.
His paintings are all sort of iconic activities or things in Portland.
So he has paintings with bridges over them, and Mount St.
Helens exploding, and the river, the Lamont, I think it is, that runs through there, and people kayaking.
And so he has all these things, and people with umbrellas in the rain and all that kind of stuff.
And they're kind of collage-y type paintings, but really humorous and interesting, colorful.
So he uses the city as his subject matter, not as realistic scenes, but as composites of various symbolic things about Portland.

So we're driving around, and he sees something he wants to look at, and he sees kids playing in the field, and so he stops over and he just looks at them for a while, because that's his topic, is Portland scenes.
And I just realize he just sees things.
An artist really does look at people, so the artist in this report, this story, knows how to see people and to see everything.
And so we could be practitioners of that art, I think, and learn to be with people and to let them feel really seen as individuals.
I have one last quotation about our common humanity now, how we all are in this together from George Saunders' new novel called *Lincoln in the Bardo*.

Lincoln, this is a work of fiction, but it's about a real occurrence that happened in Lincoln's life where his young son Willie died of typhoid fever, and Lincoln was very, very fond of him, so this was a big tragedy for him.

And the book is about people who have died who are in the Bardo, the space between life and the next life, and it's a comical book in a lot of ways, and really sweet in other ways, where these people, these spirits are running around not knowing where the hell they are kind of thing.
But on the evening of the burial of Willie, Lincoln goes to his tomb to hold him again.
I guess, I don't know if he physically held him or just to touch the tomb.
And this is Lincoln's words as, according to this writer, this novelist, Lincoln's mind was freshly inclined toward sorrow, toward the fact that the world is full of sorrow.
Everyone labored under some burden of sorrow.
All were suffering.

Whatever way one took in this world, one must try to remember that all were suffering, none content, all wronged, neglected, overlooked, misunderstood, and therefore one must do what one could to lighten the load of those with whom one came into contact.
His current state of sorrow was not uniquely his, not at all, but rather, it's like had been felt, would yet be felt by scores of others in all times, in every time.
So we have time for a couple of questions, and I was thinking also what I would really like to do is chant together the chant we don't do very often, the merging of difference and unity.
That's on page ten.
Got a book?
I think it's on page ten.
I have an old gift.
Okay.
Yeah, just a day to start us.
Thank you.
Want to do the title?
Sure, sure.
